localBiteReport: The most recent readable reports for Choctawhatchee Bay are from late June–late July 2026, so treat this as slightly dated rather than brand-new. Speckled trout have been a consistent highlight, with multiple guides around Santa Rosa Beach and the West Bay area reporting solid numbers including some quality fish; one West Bay trip in late June reported limits of large redfish alongside good trout action on the flats and backwaters. Water temps are at 86°F, which pushes the daytime bite shallow for redfish and trout — early morning, evening, and after-dark sessions around dock lights and deeper flat edges near drop-offs are the most productive windows. FishingBooker's August seasonal outlook for the bay notes that bull redfish and gator trout are the marquee summer targets, with redfish concentrating around the Hogtown Bayou flats and trout action remaining solid; flounder fishing also holds up through the summer on the bay side.

aiSummary: Choctawhatchee Bay is fishing in full summer mode today — water temps are at 86°F, which pushes redfish and trout into shaded, deeper, or cooler water during the heat of the day, making the early morning window before 9 AM and any evening session your most productive bets. Recent reports from late June through late July highlight consistent speckled trout action across the bay's grass flats and backwaters, with quality redfish also showing on the flats near West Bay and Hogtown Bayou; those patterns should still be in play, though conditions may have shifted somewhat as we move deeper into August. A 29% storm chance kicks in after 1 PM today, so plan to be off the open water or back in protected bayous by early afternoon, and keep an eye on the sky as those summer cells can build fast.

bridge.aiNote: The 331 Bridge spans the narrow neck of Choctawhatchee Bay, creating a current funnel where bait gets pushed through on both tides. Pilings hold speckled trout, redfish, sheepshead, and black drum year-round, with the lee-side pilings being the prime ambush zone on incoming tides. This is open, exposed water — it's typically the first spot on the bay to become uncomfortable or unfishable when wind and chop build.
bridge.todaysCall: With SE winds at 0–10 mph today, the bridge should be manageable early, but chop can still make piling work tricky if that wind fills in. The low tide falls around 2:42 PM, so the morning incoming tide push is your best window — work the lee-side pilings as bait gets funneled through the neck. The waning crescent and spring tidal push will strengthen that current flow, which is a real advantage here; get there at first light around 6 AM and work through mid-morning. Be off or tucked up by early afternoon given the post-1 PM storm window — open water at the bridge is no place to be when cells fire.

alaqua.aiNote: Alaqua Bayou offers protected water with a strong year-round redfish population, plus speckled trout and flounder at the mouth. The oyster bars at the creek mouth are the prime structure to target, and tree cover keeps the interior a few degrees cooler than the open bay while providing natural shelter from wind and weather. The upper creek transitions to brackish water and can hold largemouth bass alongside smaller redfish.
alaqua.todaysCall: Alaqua is a smart call today — the tree cover and protected layout help offset the brutal 86°F water temps and heat index pushing toward 102°F, giving fish and anglers alike a little relief. Hit the oyster bars at the creek mouth on the morning incoming tide and work topwaters or soft plastics along shaded edges for trout and reds; the bite will likely shut down once the sun gets high and heat peaks midday. The spring tidal push amplifies current through the mouth — that's your prime window to intercept trout and redfish ambushing bait on the bars. You'll be well-sheltered from the SE breeze here, and the enclosed layout gives you a safe bailout if afternoon storms develop after 1 PM.

basin.aiNote: Basin Bayou sees noticeably less pressure than nearby Alaqua and LaGrange, which tends to translate into less-educated fish. The interior grass flats are classic sight-fishing territory for redfish in under two feet of water. Pompano occasionally show at the mouth on moving tides in late spring and early summer, and the bayou is less protected than LaGrange when weather builds.
basin.todaysCall: The lighter pressure at Basin Bayou is a real asset in the summer heat — redfish on those shallow interior flats haven't seen as many lures as fish elsewhere. Go early: get on the grass flats at first light with the incoming tide moving and look for tailing or pushing reds in the skinny water before the sun climbs and temps push fish to edges and drop-offs. Slightly stained water today means fish will be using their lateral line as much as their eyes, so a darker soft plastic or a noisy topwater can help them home in. Keep your morning timetable tight — Basin offers less weather protection than LaGrange, so plan to wrap up or relocate well before the post-1 PM storm window.

lagrange.aiNote: LaGrange Bayou is the top trout producer among the bayous on this side of the bay — the oyster bars at the mouth are legendary, and interior grass flats hold redfish year-round. Deep holes inside the bayou hold black drum and sheepshead, rounding out a diverse fishery. It's the most protected water in this part of the bay, making it the reliable go-to when weather builds.
lagrange.todaysCall: LaGrange is arguably the best all-around choice today given the storm risk and oppressive heat — it's the most protected spot on this side of the bay and the top trout producer in recent reports. Start on the oyster bars at the mouth during the morning incoming tide with the spring tidal push amplifying current flow; that's a textbook setup for trout stacking up to ambush bait. As the tide drops toward the 2:42 PM low, shift focus to the deeper interior holes where black drum and sheepshead will hold through the heat of the day. The slightly stained water suits a slower, bottom-oriented presentation for the drum and sheepshead, and you can sit tight inside the bayou all afternoon if storms fire — it's the safest place to wait them out.

fourmile.aiNote: Four Mile Creek is a tidal creek running between Shipyard Marina and the bay, with tidal flow pushing baitfish up the creek on incoming tides and concentrating redfish and trout in the bends and along grass edges. The creek mouth is a prime flounder zone, and the upper section transitions to brackish water that can hold bass alongside smaller reds. It's a short, protected fishery and is considered the safest option on this side of the bay when weather threatens.
fourmile.todaysCall: Four Mile Creek is your safest play today if the storm outlook has you nervous — it's short, protected, and you can be off the water fast if cells develop after 1 PM. Work the creek mouth for flounder and trout on the morning incoming tide; with the spring tidal push adding strength to the flow, baitfish will be pushed up the creek and predators will stack accordingly in the bends and grass edges. SE winds at 0–10 mph shouldn't create any issues in this enclosed creek. If you're pushing into the afternoon, drop a shrimp or a slow-rolling jig along the deeper bend holes — fish will shade up as water temps peak at 86°F.

hogtown.aiNote: Hogtown Bayou is a signature Santa Rosa Beach guide destination and one of the most consistently productive trout flats on Choctawhatchee Bay. Summer mornings are peak season here, with speckled trout stacking on the grass in two to four feet of water. Spanish mackerel show at the mouth on moving tides, and the spot does see regular guide pressure despite its productivity.
hogtown.todaysCall: Recent reports specifically call out Hogtown Bayou as a marquee summer spot for speckled trout and redfish, and today's conditions set up well for an early morning session — be on the grass flats in 2–4 feet of water at first light with the incoming tide. The spring tidal push will move water briskly across the flats, which activates the trout bite; throw a suspending twitch bait or popping cork rig and work the edges methodically. Factor in run time from the 331 Bridge since Hogtown is further west — launch early and account for travel so you're fishing, not running, at prime time. Clear out before noon: open flats fishing gets tough once the heat index hits 102°F, and the post-1 PM storm window makes lingering on the water here a risk.

mallet.aiNote: Mallet Bayou is a small tributary that feeds directly into LaGrange Bayou, just south of Freeport. That direct connection to one of the bay's top trout-and-redfish producers means the same oyster-bar and grass-flat patterns likely extend into this quieter, smaller water, though documented fishing history for Mallet Bayou itself is limited. Its small, interior character makes it a natural calm-water option when wind builds on the open bay.
mallet.todaysCall: Think of Mallet Bayou today as a quieter, lower-pressure extension of LaGrange — if the oyster bars at LaGrange's mouth are crowded or blown out, slide up into Mallet to find the same species in less-pressured water. The incoming morning tide is your best window; work soft plastics or live shrimp along whatever grass edges and structure you find inside. With the spring tidal push amplifying current through LaGrange's connection to Mallet, bait movement should activate both trout and redfish. The interior location makes this a solid storm-safe option for the afternoon — just don't expect the depth of fish-holding structure you'd find in LaGrange proper.

mack.aiNote: Mack Bayou sits on the barrier-island side of Choctawhatchee Bay near Topsail Hill Preserve State Park, well west of the 331 Bridge — this is a long-run destination, not a quick local trip. It shares the protected-bayou character of Alaqua and LaGrange, with marsh grass, oyster bars, and interior holes, and sees less pressure simply due to its distance from the main boat ramps. Hewett and Buck Bayou sit immediately to the east and are realistically fishable in the same trip.
mack.todaysCall: Mack Bayou rewards the angler willing to make the run — lower pressure and the same protected bayou habitat as the top producers closer to the bridge. If you go, leave early to account for run time and be fishing the oyster bars and grass edges by first light when the incoming tide is moving and the heat hasn't set in. The SE wind at 0–10 mph shouldn't create major issues on the run west, but watch it carefully — if it builds, the return trip into the chop with afternoon storms threatening could get sporty. Combine the trip with Hewett and Buck to the east to maximize the long run; you'll have enough water to pick apart all three before the post-1 PM storm cutoff.

hewett.aiNote: Hewett Bayou sits immediately east of Mack Bayou on the barrier-island side of Choctawhatchee Bay, near Topsail Hill Preserve State Park, and is another long-run spot from the 331 Bridge that pairs naturally with Mack and Buck Bayou in the same trip. It offers the same protected-bayou habitat as its neighbors — oyster bars and marsh grass at the mouth with deeper interior holes further in. Light fishing pressure due to its distance from the main ramps is its signature advantage.
hewett.todaysCall: Hewett fishes best as part of a dedicated run to the 30-A side of the bay paired with Mack and Buck — it's too far to justify as a solo destination on a weather-uncertain day. Start early to make the run in calm morning conditions before the SE breeze has a chance to build, and work the oyster bar structure at the mouth during the incoming tide push. With spring tidal current adding flow, the mouth and any grass edges nearby are where trout and redfish will stage. Keep a hard eye on the time and sky — you'll want to begin your return run well before 1 PM given the storm window and the distance back to the ramp.

buck.aiNote: Buck Bayou is the smallest and least-documented of the three neighboring bayous on the barrier-island side of Choctawhatchee Bay near Topsail Hill Preserve State Park. Its habitat should track its larger neighbors — marsh grass, some oyster structure, and a modest interior — but there's less basis to speak confidently about its specific fish-holding character. It's best treated as a bonus stop on a Mack and Hewett Bayou trip rather than a standalone destination.
buck.todaysCall: Buck Bayou makes sense today only as a quick add-on while you're already running the 30-A side of the bay with Mack and Hewett — don't build a trip around it alone, especially on a day with a post-1 PM storm window that limits your offshore buffer time. If you do poke in, fish it the same way you'd approach its neighbors: work any oyster structure or grass edges at the mouth during the morning incoming tide and look for reds and trout using the tidal current to their advantage. Given its small size, you can pick it apart quickly and move on to Hewett or Mack for more proven water. Budget your return-run time carefully — the distance from the ramp leaves little room for weather delays.
